description: Judge benchmark input: every candidate a judge should see in a bench run. The 13 real entries are the primaries of the 2026-08-04 libexpat run with every judge-assigned field stripped (no fp_verdict, fp_rationale, severity, attack_vector, exploitability, severity_rationale, severity_validated, id, merged_into). The 8 seeded entries are from seeded_false_positives.json and are wrong on purpose.
how_to_run: Preferred: resume the cached run (Workflow with resumeFromRunId) so the hunters replay and supply the 13 real findings, and pass ONLY the 8 seeded items as injectFindings. Without a cached run to resume, pass all 21 items as injectFindings against a corpus where the hunters find nothing new. Either way score the resulting findings.json with score_judge_bench.py, which matches on (file, line, title) and does not depend on ids.

items.title: DTD/accounting state aliased (not copied) between a parameter-entity sub-parser and its parent, contradicting the documented "safe to use in a separate thread" contract
items.description: expat.h:850-853 documents that the parser returned by XML_ExternalEntityParserCreate() is "completely independent and may safely be used in a separate thread". expat.h:421-425 further documents that the `context` argument the application is expected to pass through is NULL exactly when the referenced entity is a parameter entity (i.e. the external/foreign DTD subset). But when `context` is NULL, xmlparse.c:1336-1337 takes the `newDtd = oldDtd;` branch, and parserCreate() (xmlparse.c:1029-1030 `if (dtd) parser->m_dtd = dtd;`) binds the brand-new parser's `m_dtd` field to that identical `DTD*` pointer instead of a copy. The code's own comment at xmlparse.c:1400-1407 confirms this is deliberate: "The DTD instance referenced by parser->m_dtd is shared between the document's root parser and external PE parsers". No mutex, spinlock, or any other synchronization primitive protects this shared `DTD` structure anywhere in xmlparse.c (grep for pthread/lock/mutex/spin across the whole lib/ tree returns nothing). Both the parent and the "independent" parameter-entity child mutate the very same `HASH_TABLE`s (generalEntities, paramEntities, elementTypes, attributeIds, prefixes) via `lookup()` (xmlparse.c:6864-6951), which reallocs and rehashes the table array in place, and the same `STRING_POOL`s via `poolGrow()` (xmlparse.c:7144), which reallocs pool blocks and rewrites `pool->start/end/ptr`. In addition, `accountingDiffTolerated`/`accountingOnAbort` walk up to the true root parser with `getRootParserOf()` (xmlparse.c:7617-7629) and mutate `rootParser->m_accounting.countBytesDirect/countBytesIndirect` (xmlparse.c:7519-7527) directly on that shared root struct, which the child reaches through the very same `m_parentParser` chain set at xmlparse.c:1387.
items.impact: An attacker-supplied XML document containing `<!DOCTYPE d SYSTEM "ext.dtd">` (or PUBLIC) is enough to reach the context==NULL code path: expat itself invokes `parser->m_externalEntityRefHandler(parser->m_externalEntityRefHandlerArg, 0 /* context */, entity->base, entity->systemId, entity->publicId)` at xmlparse.c:4687 and xmlparse.c:4727 for exactly this case. If the embedding application follows expat's own documented, explicitly sanctioned pattern of running the returned parser "in a separate thread" (e.g. to fetch/parse the external DTD subset off the network on a worker thread while the parent keeps parsing), the two threads race on the same `HASH_TABLE`/`STRING_POOL` realloc/rehash operations with zero synchronization -- a classic heap corruption / use-after-free / double-free primitive driven entirely by remote XML content. Even short of memory corruption, the unsynchronized `m_accounting` counter updates can desynchronize the entity-expansion (billion-laughs) amplification accounting that the library relies on as a DoS mitigation.
items.recommendation: Either add real synchronization (a lock) around the shared DTD/root-accounting state so that parent and parameter-entity-child parsers can safely run concurrently as documented, or correct the API documentation for XML_ExternalEntityParserCreate/XML_ExternalEntityRefHandler to explicitly state that the returned parser is NOT independent and must not be driven from a different thread than its parent whenever `context` was NULL.

items.title: XML_ParseBuffer() commits an unvalidated `len` to the buffer window, causing a heap out-of-bounds read
items.description: XML_ParseBuffer is the public, documented "zero-copy" streaming counterpart to XML_GetBuffer: an application calls XML_GetBuffer(parser, n) to obtain a writable pointer into the parser's internal buffer, writes bytes into it (typically from a socket/file read), and then calls XML_ParseBuffer(parser, len, isFinal) to tell the parser how many of those bytes are valid. XML_ParseBuffer performs no validation whatsoever on `len`: it neither rejects negative values nor checks that `len` does not exceed the buffer capacity actually available (`parser->m_bufferLim - parser->m_bufferEnd`). It unconditionally does `parser->m_bufferEnd += len;` and then sets `parser->m_parseEndPtr = parser->m_bufferEnd;`, which becomes the `end` pointer handed straight to the tokenizer (`parser->m_processor(parser, start, parser->m_parseEndPtr, &parser->m_bufferPtr)`). The tokenizer functions (e.g. PREFIX(contentTok) in xmltok_impl.c) trust this `end` pointer completely and scan every byte between `start` and `end` with no awareness of `m_bufferLim` at all. By contrast, the sibling function XML_GetBuffer (same file, lines 2037-2054) is careful: it checks `len < 0` (line 2040) and computes `len > EXPAT_SAFE_PTR_DIFF(parser->m_bufferLim, parser->m_bufferEnd)` (line 2054) before deciding whether to grow the buffer. XML_ParseBuffer has no equivalent check, and a grep over the file confirms `m_bufferLim` is referenced only inside XML_Parse's no-XML_CONTEXT_BYTES branch and inside XML_GetBuffer -- never inside XML_ParseBuffer or anywhere in the doContent/tokenizer call chain it feeds. So any `len` value greater than the buffer capacity that was actually allocated (e.g. the default INIT_BUFFER_SIZE = 1024 bytes on the first call, xmlparse.c:241) pushes `parser->m_parseEndPtr` past the end of the malloc'd block, and the tokenizer will read and hand to the application's SAX callbacks (CharacterDataHandler, StartElementHandler, etc.) whatever adjacent heap memory follows the buffer, until it hits the (out-of-bounds) `end` pointer or a byte that terminates the current token type.
items.impact: Heap buffer over-read reachable through a documented public API entry point that is explicitly meant to consume untrusted, application-supplied data (XML_ParseBuffer is listed in this codebase's own entry-point inventory as taking "untrusted bytes previously written into the buffer returned by XML_GetBuffer"). If the calling application derives `len` from anything other than the exact number of bytes it wrote into the buffer returned by the matching XML_GetBuffer call (a common real-world bug: reusing a network-supplied length/content-size field, forgetting to clamp a read() return value, or any mismatch between the requested buffer size and the length later committed), expat will read and parse memory beyond the allocated block. This can crash the process (DoS, e.g. hitting an unmapped guard page under a hardened allocator/ASan) or leak adjacent heap contents (other parser state, previous request/response buffers, key material, etc.) into the document as if it were legitimate XML content, exposing it via the application's registered element/attribute/character-data callbacks -- an information-disclosure primitive in addition to the crash.
items.recommendation: Validate `len` in XML_ParseBuffer exactly as XML_GetBuffer already does for the same field: reject negative values, and reject/refuse `len > EXPAT_SAFE_PTR_DIFF(parser->m_bufferLim, parser->m_bufferEnd)` before advancing `parser->m_bufferEnd`, returning XML_STATUS_ERROR (e.g. XML_ERROR_NO_MEMORY or a new dedicated error code) instead of silently accepting an out-of-range commit length.

items.title: Unchecked integer addition when folding retained context bytes into the required buffer size in XML_GetBuffer
items.description: In the XML_CONTEXT_BYTES-enabled buffer-growth path of XML_GetBuffer, `neededSize` is validated to be non-negative (xmlparse.c:2062-2065) before `keep` (clamped to at most XML_CONTEXT_BYTES at xmlparse.c:2068-2069) is added to it at line 2070 with no re-check for signed overflow. If `neededSize` is already near INT_MAX, the addition can overflow `int neededSize` to a negative value.
items.data_flow: Source: the `len` argument the embedding application passes to XML_GetBuffer (or indirectly to XML_Parse, which calls XML_GetBuffer internally) combined with the amount of already-buffered unconsumed input. Sink: the subsequent `neededSize <= EXPAT_SAFE_PTR_DIFF(parser->m_bufferLim, parser->m_buffer)` comparison at xmlparse.c:2072-2073, which decides whether to skip reallocation and instead memmove within the existing buffer.
items.reachability: Requires the embedding application to request (or have queued) a buffer size close to INT_MAX bytes; this is a property of the host application's chunking behavior rather than something a REMOTE attacker controls purely through XML content, so real-world reachability depends on how the host derives its `len` argument.
items.impact: A wrapped negative `neededSize` can make the size comparison spuriously succeed, causing the code to reuse/move data within a buffer that is in fact too small for the incoming write, i.e. a potential heap buffer overflow.
items.recommendation: Add the same guard upstream added: `if (keep > INT_MAX - neededSize) { parser->m_errorCode = XML_ERROR_NO_MEMORY; return NULL; }` before the addition.

items.title: Unchecked signed-int overflow in storeRawNames() bypasses the realloc-needed check, causing memcpy to overrun tag->buf
items.description: storeRawNames() persists a still-open start tag's raw name from the (about to be discarded/moved) parse buffer into tag->buf. It computes `bufSize = nameLen + ROUND_UP(tag->rawNameLength, sizeof(XML_Char))` (xmlparse.c:2571) as plain `int` arithmetic with no overflow check, unlike every other dynamic-size REALLOC/MALLOC call in this file (e.g. xmlparse.c:1936, 3266-3294, 3480-3489, 6245, 6902-6910, 7264-7274, 7351-7362, 7222 all carry an explicit 'Detect and prevent integer overflow' guard before sizing an allocation). Since nameLen ≈ tag->rawNameLength+1 for the common char-based XML_Char build, bufSize ≈ 2*rawNameLength+1, which overflows a 32-bit signed int once rawNameLength exceeds ~1.07 GiB (INT_MAX/2). On overflow bufSize wraps negative. The guard at xmlparse.c:2572 `if (bufSize > tag->bufEnd - tag->buf)` then compares a negative int against a positive ptrdiff_t and is false, so the REALLOC that would have grown tag->buf is skipped entirely. Execution falls through to the unconditional `memcpy(rawNameBuf, tag->rawName, tag->rawNameLength)` at xmlparse.c:2591, which still uses the full, un-overflowed tag->rawNameLength (up to ~2 GiB) as the copy length, while rawNameBuf points into the small, un-grown tag->buf allocation (previously sized only to hold the converted tag name, not the raw bytes as well).
items.data_flow: Source: attacker-supplied XML delivered via XML_Parse/XML_ParseBuffer (xmlparse.c:1818/1972) containing a single start-tag whose element name is longer than ~1.07 GiB (achievable in one call, since XML_Parse's `len` is `int` and can be up to ~2 GiB, or accumulated across multiple non-final XML_Parse calls into the internal buffer which XML_GetBuffer grows up to just under INT_MAX). XmlNameLength() (xmltok_impl.c:1726-1754) enforces no upper bound on name length. When the closing '>' of the start tag is finally seen, doContent()'s XML_TOK_START_TAG_WITH_ATTS handling (xmlparse.c:2908-2909) sets tag->rawNameLength to this huge value, then contentProcessor()/externalEntityContentProcessor() (xmlparse.c:2604-2606, 2720-2722) call storeRawNames() in the same call. There is no validation layer between XmlNameLength()'s result and its use as a memcpy length/size-arithmetic operand.
items.reachability: Directly reachable from the public XML_Parse/XML_ParseBuffer entry points with no special parser configuration (namespace mode on or off both hit this path); the only precondition is supplying an XML start tag whose name exceeds roughly 1 GiB before it is closed.
items.impact: Heap buffer overflow: memcpy writes up to ~2 GiB of attacker-controlled bytes past the end of the small `tag->buf` heap allocation, corrupting adjacent heap memory. This is a memory-corruption primitive reachable purely from untrusted XML content (REMOTE threat model), though it requires the attacker to be able to deliver roughly a gigabyte or more of contiguous tag-name data to the parser.
items.recommendation: Add the same overflow-detection idiom used everywhere else in this file before computing bufSize, e.g. compute nameLen/ROUND_UP in `unsigned`/`size_t`, check `tag->rawNameLength > (INT_MAX - nameLen)` (or equivalent) before adding, and bail out with XML_ERROR_NO_MEMORY on overflow instead of silently skipping the realloc.

items.title: Unbounded C-stack recursion via chained (non-cyclic) internal general/parameter entity references
items.description: When doContent() encounters a general-entity reference (XML_TOK_ENTITY_REF) whose entity has textPtr set (an internal entity) and default expansion is enabled, it calls processInternalEntity() synchronously (line 2864). processInternalEntity() (xmlparse.c:5552-5614) sets entity->open=TRUE and then directly calls doContent() again on the entity's replacement text (xmlparse.c:5594). If that replacement text itself contains a reference to a *different* (not-yet-open) entity, doContent() recurses into processInternalEntity() again, and so on. The only cycle guard is `if (entity->open) return XML_ERROR_RECURSIVE_ENTITY_REF;` (xmlparse.c:2850), which blocks a entity referencing itself (directly or through a cycle) but does nothing to bound the *depth* of a strictly-descending chain of distinct entities e1 -> e2 -> ... -> eN. No counter of open-entity depth (parser->m_openInternalEntities length, xmlparse.c:658/5573) is ever compared against a maximum anywhere in the file (grep across xmlparse.c confirms no such comparison exists), and expat.h exposes no API to configure a maximum entity nesting depth. The same mutual-recursion pattern also exists for parameter entities via doProlog()'s XML_ROLE_PARAM_ENTITY_REF handling (xmlparse.c:5211-5279, calling processInternalEntity at line 5274), and this entity-declaration/reference machinery is compiled unconditionally (not gated by `#ifdef XML_DTD`; confirmed by grep for `XML_ROLE_GENERAL_ENTITY_NAME`/`XML_ROLE_ENTITY_VALUE` handling at xmlparse.c:4874-4988, none of which sit inside an XML_DTD guard), so the path is present in every build configuration. The billion-laughs amplification guard (accountingDiffTolerated, xmlparse.c:7499-7551) is the only other relevant defense, but it only rejects input once total processed bytes exceed activationThresholdBytes (default 8 MiB, internal.h:142-143) AND the direct/indirect byte ratio exceeds maximumAmplificationFactor (default 100.0, internal.h:140-141). A chain of N distinct small entities, each just wrapping the previous one (e.g. `<!ENTITY eK "&e(K-1);">`), produces an amplification ratio of roughly 1.0 (no exponential blow-up) and a total byte count that stays well under 8 MiB even for tens of thousands of entities, so `accountingDiffTolerated` returns tolerated=TRUE at every step and never aborts the parse -- the guard is designed to catch exponential expansion, not linear recursion depth.
items.impact:
An attacker who controls the XML document handed to XML_Parse()/XML_ParseBuffer() (the primary, directly remote-reachable entry point per the threat model) can define on the order of 10,000-100,000 chained internal entities in a small (well under 1 MB, and definitely under the 8 MiB accounting-activation threshold) document such as:
<!DOCTYPE d [
<!ENTITY e0 "x">
<!ENTITY e1 "&e0;">
<!ENTITY e2 "&e1;">
... (repeat for N entities)
<!ENTITY eN "&e(N-1);">
]><d>&eN;</d>
Parsing the final reference &eN; drives doContent()/processInternalEntity() into N levels of mutual C-stack recursion. Because each recursion level is a full call of the large doContent() function (many local variables/switch state) plus processInternalEntity(), the native call stack (default 1-8 MiB depending on platform/thread) is exhausted well before any byte-amplification or entity-count heuristic can trigger, producing an uncontrolled stack overflow that crashes the process (or is otherwise undefined behavior) -- a remote, input-driven denial of service against any application that parses untrusted XML with expat.
items.recommendation: Track entity-expansion recursion depth explicitly (e.g., a counter incremented in processInternalEntity()/decremented on return, independent of the byte-amplification accounting) and reject XML_ERROR_ENTITY_EXPANSION-style errors once a configurable maximum depth is exceeded, the way other deeply-nested parser DoS classes are typically bounded. Alternatively, convert the internal-entity expansion path from direct recursive C calls into the same processor-trampoline/work-queue pattern expat already uses to keep normal (non-entity) parsing iterative rather than recursive.

items.title: Unchecked signed-int doubling of tag name buffer size allows overflow in doContent's start-tag conversion loop
items.description: While converting a start-tag's raw element name into tag->buf (the XML_Char-encoded copy later handed to storeAtts()/the start-element handler), the growth loop computes the next buffer size as `bufSize = (int)(tag->bufEnd - tag->buf) << 1;` and immediately calls `REALLOC(parser, tag->buf, bufSize)` / `tag->bufEnd = temp + bufSize;` with no check that the doubled value stays within a positive `int` range. Every other buffer-doubling site in this same file guards against exactly this: XML_GetBuffer's main input-buffer growth explicitly computes `bufferSize = (int)(2U * (unsigned)bufferSize)` under a "Do not invoke signed arithmetic overflow" comment and rejects `bufferSize <= 0` (xmlparse.c:2104-2109); XML_Parse's own leftover-buffer growth does `bytesToAllocate = (int)((unsigned)len * 2U)` under an "avoid _signed_ integer overflow" comment and requires `bytesToAllocate > 0` (xmlparse.c:1934-1939); defineAttribute's defaultAtts array growth has an explicit "Detect and prevent integer overflow" check (`if (type->allocDefaultAtts > INT_MAX / 2) return 0;`) before doubling (xmlparse.c:6233-6238); and poolGrow's blockSize doubling checks `if (blockSize < 0) return XML_FALSE;` after the shift (xmlparse.c:7176-7185). The tag->buf growth path at line 2927 is the sole outlier lacking this guard.
items.data_flow: Source: raw bytes of a start-tag element name in attacker-supplied XML fed to XML_Parse (xmlparse.c:1818) / XML_ParseBuffer (xmlparse.c:1972); expat's own XML_GetBuffer growth (xmlparse.c:2037-2152, itself overflow-checked) lets a single tag name span many XML_Parse calls with no inherent length cap other than available memory. Sink: bufSize used unchecked as the REALLOC size and as a pointer-arithmetic offset at xmlparse.c:2929/2933. No validation of bufSize's sign or magnitude exists between the shift at line 2927 and its use, unlike the four sibling growth sites cited above.
items.reachability: XML_Parse/XML_ParseBuffer -> parser->m_processor chain (contentProcessor/prologProcessor) -> doContent (xmlparse.c:2728) -> XML_TOK_START_TAG_NO_ATTS / XML_TOK_START_TAG_WITH_ATTS case (xmlparse.c:2883-2939) -> the tag->buf growth loop (xmlparse.c:2911-2937). Directly reachable from any XML document's first (or any) start tag; no DTD or special configuration required.
items.impact: An element start-tag name that, once converted to the internal XML_Char encoding, requires roughly 2^31 bytes (reachable by doubling repeatedly from the 32-byte INIT_TAG_BUF_SIZE) causes the left-shift to overflow a signed int, which is undefined behavior and in practice wraps to a negative bufSize. That negative int is passed as the `size_t size` parameter of `realloc_fcn` (expat.h:220): on a 64-bit build the value sign-extends to an astronomically large request that will simply fail (XML_ERROR_NO_MEMORY, safe but only after the attacker forced multi-gigabyte buffer growth); on a build where size_t is 32-bit, the same bit pattern reinterprets as a large-but-potentially-satisfiable ~2GiB allocation, and if it succeeds, `tag->bufEnd = temp + bufSize` adds a negative offset to a valid pointer, corrupting the tracked buffer bounds (tag->bufEnd ends up far below tag->buf) with undefined-behavior pointer arithmetic that subsequent XmlConvert calls use as a copy limit. At minimum this is a large-memory-allocation DoS reachable purely from an attacker-controlled start-tag element name (fed to XML_Parse/XML_ParseBuffer, whose own input buffer is grown safely across multiple calls so the tag name is not limited by a single call's `len`); on 32-bit-size_t targets it is a buffer-bounds corruption bug.
items.mitigations_checked: None present at this specific site. Confirmed absent by reading xmlparse.c:2911-2937 in full. Contrasted against confirmed present guards elsewhere in the same file: xmlparse.c:2104-2109 (XML_GetBuffer), xmlparse.c:1934-1939 (XML_Parse leftover-buffer growth), xmlparse.c:6233-6238 (defineAttribute defaultAtts growth), xmlparse.c:7176-7185 and 7218-7226 (poolGrow blockSize doubling).
items.recommendation: Mirror the guard used at every other doubling site in this file, e.g. reject the growth before shifting: `if ((tag->bufEnd - tag->buf) > (INT_MAX >> 1)) return XML_ERROR_NO_MEMORY;` prior to computing bufSize, or compute it the same overflow-safe way XML_GetBuffer does (`(int)(2U * (unsigned)(tag->bufEnd - tag->buf))` followed by a `bufSize <= 0` check) before calling REALLOC.

items.title: Namespace-separator injection in addBinding() lets an attacker-controlled URI value forge extra fields in the qualified name string
items.description: When namespace processing is enabled (XML_ParserCreateNS), expat reports element/attribute names to the application as a single XML_Char string of the form "URI SEP local[SEP prefix]", where SEP is the one-character separator the embedding application chose at parser-creation time. The namespace URI half of that string comes directly from an attacker-controlled `xmlns="..."`/`xmlns:p="..."` attribute value in the untrusted document. addBinding() validates the URI against the reserved `xml`/`xmlns` namespace strings (the `for (len = 0; uri[len]; len++)` loop at xmlparse.c:3746-3753) but never checks whether the URI itself already contains the configured separator character before that URI is concatenated with SEP + localPart (+ SEP + prefix for triplets) at xmlparse.c:3686-3693 and stored as `binding->uri` at xmlparse.c:3811-3822. Any application that reconstructs (uri, localName[, prefix]) by splitting on the separator -- the documented/expected way to consume expat's namespace-processing mode -- can therefore be handed a string with attacker-forged extra separator-delimited fields.
items.data_flow: Source: attacker-controlled `xmlns[:prefix]="..."` attribute value in untrusted XML reaching addBinding()'s `uri` parameter via startNamespaceDecl handling in doContent/doProlog (storeAtts -> addBinding, xmlparse.c:3396/3428). Sink: xmlparse.c:3686-3693 (`tagNamePtr->str = binding->uri`, built as URI+SEP+local[+SEP+prefix]) which is what XML_Parse ultimately delivers to the application's XML_StartElementHandler/attribute callbacks as the `name`/attribute-name string. No validation exists in between that rejects a URI containing the separator byte.
items.reachability: Directly reachable from XML_Parse/XML_ParseBuffer on any namespace-aware parser (XML_ParserCreateNS) processing a REMOTE, attacker-supplied document containing a namespace declaration whose URI value includes the application's chosen separator character -- no DTD, external entity, or special configuration required.
items.impact: Delimiter injection / parser-differential: the same raw bytes can be reconstructed into a different (uri, localName[, prefix]) tuple by expat's internal representation than by the host application's own splitting logic, or can defeat exact-match / prefix-match namespace-URI checks a security-sensitive consumer performs (e.g. XML-based access control, signature/SAML namespace validation) by appending attacker-chosen trailing pseudo-fields to a URI that would otherwise compare correctly. This is exactly the delimiter-injection defect the pattern-class describes: a separator the format reserves is accepted inside a value and re-emitted so two different consumers parse it differently.
items.recommendation: Reject namespace URIs that contain the parser's configured separator character before binding them, e.g. add `if (parser->m_ns && uri[len] == parser->m_namespaceSeparator) return XML_ERROR_SYNTAX;` inside the validation loop, matching the fix upstream shipped for this exact issue (their own commit comment: "...cannot be confused by an attacker putting additional namespace separator characters into namespace declarations. That would be ambiguous and not to be expected.").

items.title: Unchecked unsigned accumulation of DTD content-model name lengths can wrap contentStringLen before it gates a later allocation
items.description: While processing an `<!ELEMENT name (child1,child2,...)>` content-model declaration, doProlog accumulates the byte length of every child-element name referenced by the content model into `dtd->contentStringLen` (declared `unsigned` at xmlparse.c:385) with a plain `+=` and no overflow check. The only overflow protection in this codebase for this field is at xmlparse.c:7355-7365, which checks the final (already-accumulated) value against `(size_t)(-1)` before using it to size a malloc for the XML_Content buffer built by the content-model materializer -- it cannot detect that the accumulator itself already wrapped around during the additions at line 5386.
items.data_flow: Source: element/child-particle names inside a REMOTE attacker-supplied internal DTD subset (`<!DOCTYPE d [ <!ELEMENT ... (...)> ]>`), reachable with no external-entity fetching required. Sink: xmlparse.c:7355-7365, which allocates `dtd->contentStringLen * sizeof(XML_Char)` bytes for the content-model name-string area that the content-model materializer subsequently writes into.
items.reachability: Reachable via XML_Parse on a document containing a sufficiently large/complex `<!ELEMENT>` content model with cumulative child-name text approaching UINT_MAX bytes; impractical to reach with a small document but not restricted to any non-default configuration.
items.impact: If the unsigned accumulator wraps, the later size check at line 7355-7365 validates the small, wrapped value while the content-model writer still emits the true (larger) amount of name data into the undersized buffer -- a heap buffer overflow.
items.recommendation: Guard the accumulation the way upstream later did: `if ((size_t)nameLen > UINT_MAX - dtd->contentStringLen) return XML_ERROR_NO_MEMORY;` before `dtd->contentStringLen += (unsigned)nameLen;`.

items.title: Non-literal format-string argument passed to fprintf
items.description: fprintf() is called with a local variable (`ellipis`) in the format-string argument position instead of a string literal. The variable happens to hold the fixed text "[..]" (declared two lines above at xmlparse.c:7474: `const char ellipis[] = "[..]";`) with no `%` conversion specifiers, so no argument-count mismatch or %n write is currently possible. The defect is the pattern itself: the compiler's format-string checking (-Wformat, -Wformat-security) cannot validate a non-constant fmt argument, so any future edit to this call site (e.g. swapping in a computed/localizable ellipsis string, or reusing this helper for other diagnostic text) would silently reintroduce a format-string vulnerability with no new warning to catch it.
items.data_flow: Source: a local const char[] literal assigned once at xmlparse.c:7474, never attacker-influenced in the code as written. Sink: fprintf(stderr, ellipis) at xmlparse.c:7490, where the second argument is the interpreted format string. Nothing between source and sink validates that the value used as a format string is actually a literal/constant; the safety here rests entirely on the fact that no one has yet put attacker- or config-derived text into that variable.
items.reachability: This call is compiled only when XML_DTD is defined (guard at xmlparse.c:7422 `#ifdef XML_DTD`, matching #endif at xmlparse.c:8153; no build system is present in this corpus to confirm whether XML_DTD is on by default). At runtime it additionally requires accountingDiffTolerated() to be invoked with rootParser->m_accounting.debugLevel >= 2 (xmlparse.c:7545) so accountingReportDiff() is called at all, and debugLevel is set only from the EXPAT_ACCOUNTING_DEBUG environment variable via getDebugLevel() (xmlparse.c:1157, 8156-8171) with the internal check `rootParser->m_accounting.debugLevel < 1` returning early otherwise (xmlparse.c:7443, called from accountingReportStats invoked at 7546). No path from untrusted XML content alone reaches this line; an operator must opt in via environment variable at process start. So while the pattern matches the format-string class exactly, it is not remotely triggerable by XML content in the code as written today.
items.impact: Currently none in practice: the runtime value is a hardcoded constant containing no conversion specifiers, so there is no information leak or %n write today, and the call site additionally requires an operator-set debug environment variable plus XML_DTD to be compiled in. This is reported as a code-hygiene / defense-in-depth finding for the format-string class rather than a demonstrated live vulnerability: the invariant that format arguments must be literals is violated, and a judge may want to rate it accordingly (informational/low) given the lack of attacker control and the debug-only gating.
items.recommendation: Replace `fprintf(stderr, ellipis)` with `fprintf(stderr, "%s", ellipis)` (or `fputs(ellipis, stderr)`) so the format-string argument is always a literal and the compiler's format-string checks stay meaningful at this call site regardless of future edits.

items.title: open("/dev/urandom", O_RDONLY) missing O_CLOEXEC lets the descriptor leak across fork+exec
items.description: writeRandomBytes_dev_urandom() opens /dev/urandom with a bare O_RDONLY (no O_CLOEXEC) and no compensating fcntl(fd, F_SETFD, FD_CLOEXEC) call, then reads into the caller-supplied buffer and closes the fd (expat/lib/xmlparse.c:797). This function runs on the entropy-fallback path used by generate_hash_secret_salt() (expat/lib/xmlparse.c:921-925), which is invoked from startParsing() (expat/lib/xmlparse.c:948-952) the first time XML_Parse()/XML_ParseBuffer() is called on a root parser, i.e. once per XML_ParserCreate lifetime, on any build where XML_DEV_URANDOM is defined, _WIN32 is not defined, and neither arc4random_buf nor arc4random is available (the getrandom()/syscall(SYS_getrandom) path is tried first and only falls through to this one if that's also unavailable). If the host application is multithreaded and another thread calls fork()+exec() while this fd is open, the child process inherits the /dev/urandom file descriptor.
items.impact: A leaked /dev/urandom descriptor in a forked child is low severity on its own (it doesn't disclose sensitive process data), but in sandboxed or fd-accounted environments an unexpected inherited descriptor can violate fd-hygiene assumptions the embedding application relies on, and repeated leaks (e.g. a server re-forking workers while parsers are concurrently created) could contribute to descriptor exhaustion. The race window is narrow (open-read-close, a handful of instructions) and requires a concurrent fork+exec from a different thread precisely during that window, so exploitability is limited; this is reported for completeness of the open-issues class rather than as a high-impact finding. Note this is a self-triggered code path (parser initialization), not something a remote XML sender can directly time, so the REMOTE threat model applies only weakly here -- the fix is still a straightforward hardening improvement.
items.recommendation: Pass O_CLOEXEC in the open() flags (open("/dev/urandom", O_RDONLY | O_CLOEXEC)), guarded by a feature check for platforms lacking O_CLOEXEC, matching the pattern the getrandom()-based sibling function already avoids needing (getrandom() has no fd to leak).

items.title: writeRandomBytes_dev_urandom() only retries when errno happens to equal EINTR, not whenever bytes are still missing
items.description: The retry loop's continuation condition is `while (! success && (errno == EINTR))` instead of simply `while (! success)` with a separate error check. POSIX read(2) is explicitly permitted to return a positive, successful short count when a signal interrupts the transfer after some bytes have already been copied; in that case errno is left untouched by the successful call, so it still holds whatever value was ambient before writeRandomBytes_dev_urandom() was entered (very likely not EINTR). When that happens the do-while exits after a single short read even though bytesWrittenTotal < count, and the function returns 0 (failure) despite having made real, uncorrupted progress. Separately, open() at line 779 is not retried on EINTR at all -- if the open() call itself is interrupted by a signal, the function bails out immediately instead of retrying, even though open() is a blocking call subject to the same EINTR contract.
items.impact: writeRandomBytes_dev_urandom() is the last high-quality entropy source tried by generate_hash_secret_salt() (xmlparse.c:899-925) before the code falls back to `gather_time_entropy() ^ getpid()` (xmlparse.c:929), which the source itself documents as near-zero-entropy ("Process ID is 0 bits entropy if attacker has local access", line 928; "<20 bits entropy", line 882). A spuriously-failed /dev/urandom read therefore silently downgrades the per-parser SipHash secret salt (xmlparse.c:6850-6855) that is the sole defense against hash-flooding DoS via attacker-chosen XML element/attribute names -- an attacker who can predict or narrow the salt can construct colliding names to degrade the internal hash tables algorithmically. This fallback path is realistic in practice: it is the effective primary entropy source on systems without arc4random_buf/arc4random/getrandom (older glibc, musl before arc4random support, pre-3.17 kernels, or containers whose seccomp profile blocks the getrandom syscall), which is a common deployment shape for an embedded library like expat.
items.recommendation: Base loop continuation purely on `bytesWrittenTotal < count`; only additionally guard on `errno == EINTR` in the specific branch where read() returned -1 (a hard failure), and otherwise treat any non-EINTR error as terminal. Wrap the open() call in the same kind of EINTR-aware retry.

items.title: gather_time_entropy() discards gettimeofday()'s failure return under NDEBUG and returns a possibly-uninitialized value
items.description: gettimeofday(&tv, NULL) at line 874 can fail (return -1) without populating `tv`, which is declared uninitialized at line 871. The only check of the return value is `assert(gettimeofday_res == 0)` (line 879), which is compiled out entirely whenever NDEBUG is defined -- the standard configuration for release builds. In that configuration, on failure the code falls straight through to `return tv.tv_usec;` (line 883) and returns whatever garbage was already on the stack, without ever detecting or reporting the failure.
items.impact: This feeds directly into the same hash-secret-salt fallback chain as the writeRandomBytes_dev_urandom finding above (generate_hash_secret_salt(), xmlparse.c:929), so a failure here would compound weakening of the SipHash key used against hash-flooding DoS. In practice gettimeofday(&tv, NULL) with a valid stack pointer and a NULL timezone argument essentially cannot fail on any current POSIX implementation (the only documented failure is EFAULT for a bad pointer, which cannot occur here), so real-world exploitability is close to nil; this is reported as a genuine ignored-return-value / use-of-uninitialized-value defect rather than a practically reachable one.
items.recommendation: Initialize `tv` (e.g. `struct timeval tv = {0};`) so a gettimeofday() failure yields a defined-but-still-weak value instead of undefined behavior, and treat a nonzero return the same way in both NDEBUG and debug builds.

items.title: XML Name/NameStart tokenizer macros accept invalid (overlong) multi-byte UTF-8 as legal name characters, while the same bytes are rejected as content
items.function: CHECK_NAME_CASE (macro; expanded into PREFIX(scanLt), PREFIX(scanPi), PREFIX(scanEndTag), PREFIX(scanRef), PREFIX(scanAtts), PREFIX(contentTok), PREFIX(prologTok))
items.description: For multi-byte UTF-8 lead bytes, CHECK_NAME_CASE (line 68-77) and CHECK_NMSTRT_CASE (line 97-106) decide whether a byte sequence is a legal XML Name/NameStart character purely via `IS_NAME_CHAR`/`IS_NMSTRT_CHAR`, which look the raw bit-pattern up in the `namingBitmap`/`namePages`/`nmstrtPages` tables (xmltok.c UTF8_GET_NAMING2/3) without ever checking that the byte sequence is a well-formed (minimal-length, in-range trailing bytes) UTF-8 encoding. The encoding's own `isInvalid2/3/4` check (`IS_INVALID_CHAR`, xmltok.c:276-281, backed by UTF8_INVALID2/3/4 which reject overlong/out-of-range sequences) exists and is correctly consulted at other tokenizer call sites for the very same byte classes -- e.g. `PREFIX(cdataSectionTok)`'s content-data loop at xmltok_impl.c:399 (`if (end - ptr < n || IS_INVALID_CHAR(enc, ptr, n))`) and the equivalent at xmltok_impl.c:874, plus INVALID_CASES/INVALID_LEAD_CASE at xmltok_impl.c:47-66 -- but is never called from CHECK_NAME_CASE/CHECK_NMSTRT_CASE. I confirmed via the actual namingBitmap/nmstrtPages/namePages tables shipped in this corpus (nametab.h) that this is exploitable, not merely theoretical: simulating UTF8_INVALID2 and UTF8_GET_NAMING2 over all BT_LEAD2 byte pairs (0xC0-0xDF lead byte x 0x00-0xFF trail byte) finds 3144 byte pairs that are invalid UTF-8 yet pass the NameStart bitmap check, 54 of which are syntactically well-formed-looking overlong 2-byte sequences (lead byte 0xC0/0xC1 with a valid 0x80-0xBF trailing byte) -- e.g. bytes 0xC1 0x81, an overlong (non-canonical) 2-byte encoding of ASCII 'A' that RFC 3629/strict UTF-8 decoders must reject.
items.code:
#  define CHECK_NAME_CASE(n, enc, ptr, end, nextTokPtr)                        \
  case BT_LEAD##n:                                                             \
    if (end - ptr < n)                                                         \
      return XML_TOK_PARTIAL_CHAR;                                             \
    if (! IS_NAME_CHAR(enc, ptr, n)) {                                         \
      *nextTokPtr = ptr;                                                       \
      return XML_TOK_INVALID;                                                  \
    }                                                                          \
    ptr += n;                                                                  \
    break;
items.data_flow: Source: raw untrusted bytes of an element/attribute/entity/notation/PI-target name in the XML_Parse/XML_ParseBuffer input stream. Sink: PREFIX(scanLt) (xmltok_impl.c:730 CHECK_NMSTRT_CASES, :756 CHECK_NAME_CASES) accepts the malformed bytes as part of a Name token; xmlparse.c's XmlConvert/XmlUtf8Convert path (utf8_toUtf8 in xmltok.c, a plain memcpy with no re-validation) copies the raw bytes verbatim into the parser's internal name buffer, which is then handed to the application's XML_StartElementHandler/attribute handlers unmodified.
items.reachability: Directly reachable from XML_Parse on a REMOTE, attacker-supplied UTF-8 document (the default/most common encoding) with no special parser configuration: a 5-byte document `3C C1 81 2F 3E` (`<` + overlong 0xC1 0x81 + `/` + `>`) is accepted by PREFIX(scanLt) as a well-formed empty element whose name is the 2-byte overlong sequence.
items.impact: Well-formedness/parser-differential bug: expat treats a document containing invalid, non-canonical (overlong) UTF-8 byte sequences inside Names as well-formed XML and forwards the raw malformed bytes to the application as part of an element/attribute/entity name, while the exact same bytes are correctly rejected (XML_TOK_INVALID / XML_ERROR_INVALID_TOKEN) when they appear as ordinary character data. Any other UTF-8-aware component in a security-relevant pipeline (a strict decoder, a second parser, a WAF/sanitizer, a canonicalizer) that correctly rejects or differently decodes overlong UTF-8 will disagree with expat about the identity/validity of the same document -- the classic parser-confusion/smuggling primitive historically associated with overlong UTF-8 encodings (cf. CWE-176/CWE-436), and a violation of XML 1.0's requirement that documents be encoded per Unicode's well-formed UTF-8 definition.
items.recommendation: Add `IS_INVALID_CHAR(enc, ptr, n) ||` to the condition in both CHECK_NAME_CASE (line 72) and CHECK_NMSTRT_CASE (line 101), and to the equivalent inline LEAD_CASE block used for standalone NAME/NMTOKEN tokens (xmltok_impl.c:1145/1150), so that Name-character scanning rejects the same invalid byte sequences that content-character scanning already rejects.

items.why_wrong: The guard is at xmlparse.c:7264 — `if (dtd->scaffSize > UINT_MAX / 2u) return -1;` — thirteen lines above the REALLOC, with a second size_t product guard at 7272 under `#if UINT_MAX >= SIZE_MAX`. The doubling cannot reach the multiplication unless it is provably safe. The finding cites the REALLOC and states the guard is absent; opening the function refutes it.
items.title: Unguarded doubling of scaffSize overflows the content-scaffold allocation
items.description: nextScaffoldPart grows the DTD content-model scaffold by doubling: `dtd->scaffSize * 2 * sizeof(CONTENT_SCAFFOLD)`. scaffSize is an unsigned int driven entirely by how many content-model particles the document's DTD declares. Once it passes UINT_MAX/2 the doubling wraps, the product passed to REALLOC is far smaller than the caller believes, and `dtd->scaffSize *= 2` on the next line records the large value anyway. Every subsequent `dtd->scaffold[next]` write at line 7292 indexes past the end of the shrunken allocation.
items.data_flow: Source: element content model in an internal or external DTD subset. Sink: the size argument to REALLOC at xmlparse.c:7278. Between them: nothing — the growth path performs no bound on scaffSize.
items.reachability: XML_Parse -> doProlog -> the element-declaration states -> nextScaffoldPart, on any document with a DTD. Reached on the first `<!ELEMENT>` declaration and on every particle thereafter.
items.impact: Heap buffer overflow with attacker-chosen contents: the scaffold entries written after the undersized realloc carry attacker-controlled type, quant, firstchild and nextsib fields.
items.mitigations_checked: Looked for an overflow check on scaffSize before the multiplication and found none; the surrounding growth sites in this file carry a 'Detect and prevent integer overflow' comment and this one does not.
items.recommendation: Reject the growth when scaffSize exceeds UINT_MAX/2, and separately when the size_t product would wrap.

items.why_wrong: keyeq stops at the first mismatching byte, and a NUL in the shorter string either matches the other string's NUL (returning XML_TRUE at 6835) or mismatches and exits the loop. Neither pointer can advance past the NUL of the shorter operand, so there is no read past any allocation. The loop looks unbounded and is not.
items.title: keyeq compares hash-table keys with no length bound
items.description: keyeq walks two key pointers in lockstep with no length parameter and no end pointer. The keys it is handed come from the string pools, which are grown block by block and are not zero-filled, so a key whose terminating NUL is missing or overwritten lets the loop advance both pointers past the end of the pool block. The comparison then reads heap memory outside either allocation until it happens on a differing byte.
items.data_flow: Source: element, attribute, prefix and entity names taken from document bytes and interned via poolStoreString. Sink: the two dereferences in the keyeq loop at xmlparse.c:6833.
items.reachability: Every lookup() call on every name in the document reaches keyeq once per probe: xmlparse.c:6888 in the collision loop.
items.impact: Out-of-bounds heap read. Under a fuzzer or a hardened allocator this is a crash; in production it is an oracle for the contents of adjacent pool blocks, observable through which names the parser treats as equal.
items.mitigations_checked: There is no length argument, no end pointer and no bound of any kind on either side of the comparison.
items.recommendation: Pass the interned length alongside the key and compare with an explicit bound.

items.why_wrong: `p` is the argument to the public API function XML_SetBase, which only the embedding application calls; no path in expat/lib passes document bytes to it (grep for XML_SetBase in lib/ finds the definition and nothing else, and m_curBase is only ever read out to handlers). Under the REMOTE threat model the attacker supplies document bytes, not the base URI. The finding asserts attacker control over a parameter the application owns.
items.title: Attacker-controlled base URI is copied into the DTD pool with no length limit
items.description: XML_SetBase copies its argument into the DTD string pool with poolCopyString, which grows the pool a block at a time until the whole NUL-terminated string fits. There is no length cap and no accounting: the base URI is copied in full however long it is, and the pool block is never released until the parser is freed. A long base string therefore turns into a proportional, retained heap allocation.
items.data_flow: Source: the base URI accompanying an external entity, which reaches the embedding application's ExternalEntityRefHandler and is handed straight back to XML_SetBase. Sink: poolCopyString at xmlparse.c:1543.
items.reachability: Any document declaring an external entity drives the external-entity handler, and the conventional handler implementation calls XML_SetBase with the system identifier it was given.
items.impact: Remote memory exhaustion: each external entity reference adds an unbounded, retained allocation to the DTD pool.
items.mitigations_checked: No length check on p, no cap on the pool, and the DTD pool is not cleared between entities. XML_SetBase does not consult the billion-laughs accounting either.
items.recommendation: Cap the base URI length, or account for it in the amplification budget.

items.why_wrong: The list pointer is advanced at xmlparse.c:1445 — `tagList = tagList->parent;` — one line BEFORE the first FREE. Nothing dereferences p after the free; `p->buf` and `p->bindings` are read at 1446 and 1447 while p is still live, and `FREE(parser, p)` is the last statement of the iteration. The finding transposes two adjacent lines.
items.title: XML_ParserFree walks the tag list through a freed node
items.description: The tag-list teardown loop frees the current node and then follows its parent pointer to reach the next one. After `FREE(parser, p)` the memory holding p->parent has been returned to the allocator, so the next iteration reads a link out of a freed chunk. With a custom XML_Memory_Handling_Suite that scrubs or reuses freed blocks — which the public API explicitly supports — the traversal follows a pointer the allocator has already overwritten.
items.data_flow: Source: tag nesting depth, entirely attacker-controlled. Sink: the freed-node dereference on the following iteration of the loop at xmlparse.c:1436.
items.reachability: XML_ParserFree is called on every parser teardown, and the tag stack is non-empty whenever parsing stopped inside an element — which an attacker arranges by truncating the document mid-element.
items.impact: Use-after-free during teardown, with the freed chunk's contents deciding where the traversal goes next.
items.mitigations_checked: No copy of the parent pointer is taken before the free, and the loop condition re-reads the list head each iteration.
items.recommendation: Save the parent pointer into a local before freeing the node.

items.why_wrong: Both `p[-1]` reads are guarded by `p != publicId` in the same condition, at xmlparse.c:6525 and again at 6532, and C's && is a sequence point, so the read never happens at the start of the buffer. The finding cites 6525 — the line that contains the guard it says is missing.
items.title: normalizePublicId reads one element before the start of publicId
items.description: normalizePublicId collapses runs of whitespace in place, keeping a write cursor p behind the read cursor s. When the very first character of the public identifier is a space, a carriage return or a newline, the whitespace branch inspects p[-1] while p is still equal to publicId, reading the byte immediately before the buffer. The buffer is the string pool block, so the read lands on the previous pool entry or on the allocator's own header.
items.data_flow: Source: the public identifier of a DOCTYPE, an entity declaration or a notation declaration, taken verbatim from the document. Sink: the p[-1] read at xmlparse.c:6525.
items.reachability: XML_Parse -> doProlog -> normalizePublicId, on any document whose public identifier begins with whitespace, e.g. `<!DOCTYPE a PUBLIC " x" "y">`.
items.impact: One-byte out-of-bounds heap read whose value steers whether a space is emitted, making it weakly observable through the normalized identifier handed to the notation handler.
items.mitigations_checked: The loop starts with p == publicId and the whitespace branch is entered on the first iteration for a leading space; no separate first-character case exists.
items.recommendation: Handle the leading-whitespace case before entering the loop.

items.why_wrong: The allocation is checked at xmlparse.c:6876-6879, immediately before the memset: `if (! table->v) { table->size = 0; return NULL; }`. The finding cites the memset at 6880 and claims no check precedes it, which the four lines above it contradict.
items.title: lookup memsets the hash table without checking the allocation
items.description: On first insertion lookup allocates the bucket array through the memory suite's malloc_fcn and then immediately zeroes it with memset. The allocation result is used as the destination without being tested, so an allocation failure — which the memory suite is entitled to report by returning NULL, and which an attacker induces by driving the parser's memory use up with a large document — turns into a write to address zero.
items.data_flow: Source: memory pressure driven by document size. Sink: the memset destination at xmlparse.c:6880.
items.reachability: Every first name interned into any of the parser's six hash tables reaches this branch: lookup is called from storeAtts, addBinding, doProlog and the entity paths.
items.impact: Null pointer dereference on a write, i.e. a remotely triggerable crash.
items.mitigations_checked: No NULL test between the malloc_fcn call and the memset; the rest of the function checks its allocations.
items.recommendation: Test the allocation before zeroing it, as the growth path further down the function does.

items.why_wrong: The loop is a do/while with the increment in the condition: the iteration that runs when *s is the NUL appends it via poolAppendChar and only then does `while (*s++)` evaluate false. The terminator is written. Rewriting the same loop as a while-loop would have the bug the finding describes; the code is not written that way.
items.title: poolCopyString returns a string that is not NUL-terminated
items.description: poolCopyString appends characters from s while the condition `*s++` holds, which stops as soon as the NUL is reached — so the terminator itself is never appended. poolFinish then closes the pool entry over the characters written, and the returned pointer is used everywhere as a C string: by keyeq, by hash, and by the handlers the application registers. Each of those reads past the end of the entry until it finds a zero byte belonging to something else.
items.data_flow: Source: entity names, notation names and system identifiers copied out of the document. Sink: every C-string consumer of the pool entry, starting with keylen at xmlparse.c:6842.
items.reachability: Reached from setContext, XML_SetBase and the entity-declaration paths, i.e. on any document with a DTD.
items.impact: Out-of-bounds heap read, and hash-table keys that compare equal to strings they should not, since the comparison runs past the intended end.
items.mitigations_checked: No explicit poolAppendChar of a terminator after the loop, and poolFinish does not add one.
items.recommendation: Append the terminating NUL explicitly after the copy loop.

items.why_wrong: Both addends are bounded immediately above the assignment: xmlparse.c:3266 rejects `n > INT_MAX - nDefaultAtts`, and 3278-3281 rejects `nDefaultAtts > INT_MAX - INIT_ATTS_SIZE` and `n > INT_MAX - (nDefaultAtts + INIT_ATTS_SIZE)`. The sum at 3283 cannot overflow, and the size_t product is guarded again at 3290.
items.title: storeAtts computes m_attsSize with an unchecked int addition
items.description: m_attsSize is recomputed as `n + nDefaultAtts + INIT_ATTS_SIZE` in signed int arithmetic. n is the attribute count returned by the tokenizer for this element and nDefaultAtts comes from the element declaration, both attacker-driven; INIT_ATTS_SIZE is added on top. Signed overflow here is undefined, and in practice yields a negative m_attsSize that the following REALLOC converts to an enormous size_t, or a small positive value that under-allocates the array the rest of the function then fills.
items.data_flow: Source: the attribute list of a start tag plus the defaulted attributes of its element declaration. Sink: the addition at xmlparse.c:3283 and the REALLOC size at 3297.
items.reachability: XML_Parse -> doContent -> storeAtts on every start tag in a namespace-aware or plain parse.
items.impact: Undersized attribute array followed by in-bounds-looking writes across it — heap corruption with attacker-controlled attribute names and values.
items.mitigations_checked: The addition itself carries no check; the only nearby test compares the result against m_attsSize after it has already been computed.
items.recommendation: Bound n and nDefaultAtts against INT_MAX before summing them.
